rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **EMF vs Terminal Voltage:** EMF ($\mathcal{E}$) is the open-circuit voltage (no current). Terminal voltage $V = \mathcal{E} - Ir$ under discharge; $V = \mathcal{E} + Ir$ during charging. The sign of the $Ir$ term depends on current direction.  ·  **Series/Parallel Cell Rules:** In series: $\mathcal{E}_{total} = \sum \mathcal{E}_i$, $r_{total} = \sum r_i$. In parallel (identical cells): $\mathcal{E}_{total} = \mathcal{E}$, $r_{total} = r/n$. These assume no circulating currents between mismatched cells.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: EMF is not a force - it is a voltage (energy per unit charge). The name is historical. EMF is measured in volts, not newtons.  ·  Terminal voltage $V = \\\\mathcal{E} - Ir$ is less than EMF when current flows out of the cell. But when charging the cell, current flows into the positive terminal, so $V = \\\\mathcal{E} + Ir$ - the terminal voltage is greater than EMF.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The internal resistance of a typical AA alkaline cell is about 0.15 $\\\Omega$ when fresh, but increases to 0.5 $\\\Omega$ or more as it discharges.  ·  Connecting cells in series increases the available voltage while keeping the same current capacity. Connecting in parallel increases the current capacity while keeping the same voltage.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **EMF ($\\\\mathcal{E}$):** the open-circuit voltage of a source. It is the work done per unit charge in moving charge around the complete circuit.  ·  **Internal resistance $r$:** the resistance inside the cell due to electrolyte and electrodes. It causes the terminal voltage to drop when current flows.  ·  **Terminal voltage:** $V = \\\\mathcal{E} - Ir$. When no current flows ($I=0$), $V = \\\\mathcal{E}$. Under load, $V < \\\\mathcal{E}$.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Concept 5: Connection between EMF and Internal Resistance and other topics  ·  **Maximum Power Transfer Theorem:** Maximum power to load $R$ occurs at $R = r$, giving $P_{max} = \mathcal{E}^2/(4r)$. At this point, efficiency is 50%. For efficiency $>50\%$, need $R > r$; for $>90\%$, need $R > 9r$.  ·  In series, both EMF and internal resistance add. In parallel, the equivalent EMF is the same as one cell, but the equivalent internal resistance is reduced, allowing more current.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Maximum power transfer ($R = r$) occurs at 50% efficiency. For efficient power delivery, you want $R \\\\gg r$ (high efficiency, low power). For maximum power, you sacrifice efficiency.  ·  A fresh battery has a high open-circuit voltage (close to its EMF) but drops significantly under load if its internal resistance has increased with age. That is why old batteries seem weak.  ·  Carefully distinguish between similar-looking concepts in emf and internal resistance.
